title: Lost and found
hookLine: finders must announce and return what they find

lines: A GLOVE ON A FENCE POST.
THE OX, THE GARMENT, ANY LOST THING.
cards: A single glove, hung on a fence post at eye level. Someone found it on the sidewalk and put it where its owner might walk back past. A small, wordless kindness, and the Torah has words for it.
Deuteronomy says that if you see your neighbor's ox or sheep wandering off, you bring it back. Then the circle widens: a donkey, a garment, anything your neighbor lost and you found.
And the passage ends with a short line, in the old JPS translation: "thou mayest not hide thyself."

teach.b: Hashavat aveidah. Returning a lost thing. Start with what the verse forbids.
Not stealing; that's covered elsewhere. It forbids hiding yourself: looking away, walking past as if you hadn't seen. This commandment begins in the eyes.
The Mishnah, in the tractate Bava Metzia, builds that line into a working system. First: which finds do you have to announce?

teach.h: SIMANIM: SIGNS THAT MAKE IT CLAIMABLE.
teach.b: The answer turns on signs, simanim in Hebrew.
Coins scattered loose on a road carry nothing to tell them apart, so the finder may keep them.
But money in a purse, fruit in a basket, a thing with a mark on it: those must be announced, because someone can say, that's mine, and here's how I know. Second, the announcing.

The Mishnah records a debate between rabbis over how long to keep announcing, and the Talmud remembers a stone in Jerusalem where finds were proclaimed and owners came to claim them. Third, who gets it back?
The claimant describes the signs, and if they match, it goes home. Behind it all sits a question the Talmud turns over at length: when has an owner given up?
The rabbis call it yeush, despair. So the system holds two people in view: the owner's hope and the finder's honesty. A law about gloves and purses is also a law about attention.
For a little while, your neighbor's loss is your job.

how: Jews who keep halacha treat returning lost property as a commandment, announcing finds that carry identifying signs and returning them when an owner describes them; some synagogues and communities keep lost-and-found notices for this reason.

o: the rule that a finder may keep any found item
the duty to return a lost thing to its owner
a prayer said when something precious goes missing

games.q: the lost-and-found law — tap the pairs.

s: the verse only forbids stealing what you find
it forbids hiding yourself: looking away when you see what someone lost.
the Mishnah says every find must be announced
coins scattered loose, with nothing to tell them apart, may be kept by the finder.
a claimant has to describe the signs
if the signs match, the find goes home.

games.q: you find a purse with money in it on a busy road. what does the Mishnah say to do?
o: keep it. nobody can prove it's theirs.
announce it. a purse is a sign someone can name.
games.why: the Mishnah lists money in a purse among the finds that must be announced. a container is a sign, so an owner can claim it.

practice: Look around your life for one thing that isn't yours: a borrowed book, a neighbor's container, a charger that drifted into your bag. Picture the moment it goes back, and the small relief on the other person's face.
If nothing comes to mind, picture the other side: something you found, hung where its owner could see it.

wordCard.voice: Hashavat aveidah. Returning a lost thing: the duty not to hide yourself when you see what someone else has lost. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the returning of a lost thing.

carryVoice: Your line: return it. The verse asks for your eyes first, then your hands. Until tomorrow.
